meta.title: The Bloop: The Loudest Mystery the Ocean Ever Recorded
meta.logline: In 1997 hydrophones across the Pacific caught a sound nobody could identify. It took eight years to learn what it really was.
meta.thesis: The ocean is so poorly mapped by sound that a cracking iceberg passed for a monster for eight years.
meta.curiosity_gap: What made a sound that hydrophones thousands of kilometres apart all heard?
meta.narrator: Spokojny, rzeczowy narrator dokumentalny w 3. osobie. Niski ton, krótkie zdania, zero sensacji bez dowodu.
meta.audience_relation: Prowadzi widza przez akta jak śledczy. Czasem zwraca się na 'you' w kluczowych momentach.
meta.bans: Zero lania wody. Żadnych zmyślonych nazwisk, dat, liczb i cytatów. Nie udawaj, że rekonstrukcja to archiwum.
meta.visual_style: 1990s archival documentary photograph, black and white, film grain, vignette, high contrast
meta.master_outline: 1) Cold open: the sound. 2) Who was listening and why. 3) Why it looked like an animal. 4) The answer: ice (2005). 5) Why it still matters.

facts.claim: In 1997 NOAA researchers listening for underwater volcanic activity in the southern Pacific recorded a mysterious sound later named 'the Bloop'.
facts.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — What is the Bloop?

facts.claim: The Bloop was picked up by hydrophones placed more than 3,219 km apart across the Pacific (over three thousand kilometres).
facts.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — What is the Bloop?

facts.claim: Based on the direction the sound arrived from, NOAA estimates the source was most likely between the Bransfield Strait and the Ross Sea, or possibly at Cape Adare, Antarctica.
In 2005, after placing hydrophones closer to Antarctica, NOAA researchers found the Bloop was an icequake: an iceberg cracking and breaking away from an Antarctic glacier.
facts.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — What is the Bloop?

facts.claim: Popular claims said the Bloop was much louder than a blue whale, the loudest known animal, and must have come from a giant unknown creature.
facts.source: Popular Science — The sea monster goes 'bloop'—or does it?

facts.claim: Analyst listening to the recording in a dim lab at night.
Early guesses about the Bloop included secret military exercises, ship engines, fishing boat winches, giant squids and whales.
facts.source: NOAA National Ocean Service — What is the Bloop?

facts.claim: NOAA's public recording of the Bloop is sped up 16 times so human ears can hear it.
NOAA oceanographer Chris Fox said in 2001 that he suspected ice off the coast of Antarctica.
facts.source: Popular Science — The sea monster goes 'bloop'—or does it?

facts.claim: Icequakes are loud enough to be detected on multiple sensors at a range of over 5,000 km.
NOAA hydrophones in the Scotia Sea recorded icequakes with spectrograms very similar to the Bloop and used them to track iceberg A53a as it broke apart near South Georgia Island in early 2008.

beats.action: Who was listening: NOAA researchers tracking underwater volcanoes. What hydrophones normally hear and the early guesses.
beats.goal: The viewer understands the tools and why an unknown sound was rare.
beats.narration: The listeners were NOAA researchers. Their hydrophones, underwater microphones, sat in the southern Pacific for one reason: to hear underwater volcanoes. Most days the tapes were predictable. Rumbles from the seafloor. Whale song. The churn of propellers. Every sound had a shape, and every shape had a name. This one didn't. The guesses came fast. Secret military exercises. Ship engines. Fishing boat winches. Giant squids. Whales.

beats.action: Show how the 'too loud for an animal' idea spread.
beats.goal: The viewer sees why people believed it was alive, labelled as speculation.
beats.narration: Then the story left the lab. Online, the Bloop grew teeth. The claim went like this: it was much louder than a blue whale, the loudest animal we know, so something bigger had to be down there. No one had a body. No one had a photo. But a sound with no name is easy to fill with a monster.

beats.action: Place the source: the arrival direction points not to the open sea but toward Antarctica. A NOAA scientist already suspects ice.
beats.goal: The viewer understands how remote the source was.
beats.narration: But the data pointed somewhere colder. Traced by the direction it arrived from, the sound came from the far south: between the Bransfield Strait and the Ross Sea, maybe Cape Adare. Antarctica. And in 2001, NOAA oceanographer Chris Fox said what the monster theory didn't want to hear. He suspected ice.

beats.action: Reveal: 2005, hydrophones closer to Antarctica, the Bloop was an icequake.
beats.goal: The viewer learns the real explanation.
beats.narration: To be sure, they had to get closer. NOAA placed hydrophones nearer to Antarctica and listened again. In 2005, the answer came back. Not a creature. Not a submarine. An icequake. An iceberg cracking and breaking away from an Antarctic glacier. Later recordings of breaking ice drew a very similar shape on paper. The monster was the sound of a glacier letting go.

beats.action: Reflect: the same method now tracks icebergs breaking apart; how much of the ocean we only hear, never see.
beats.goal: The viewer leaves with a lingering question.
beats.narration: The same ears are still listening. In early 2008, NOAA hydrophones followed an iceberg called A53a as it broke apart near South Georgia Island, one crack at a time. Icequakes like these can reach sensors over 5,000 km away. So the loudest mystery the ocean ever recorded was never hidden. It was simply far away. And somewhere out there, the ice is still talking.
